subject: Cooking
title: Nutmeg: The Spice That Caused a Genocide
description: A 60-second lesson on Nutmeg: The Spice That Caused a Genocide.

hook.text: In 1621, the Dutch massacred the population of the Banda Islands to monopolize nutmeg production.

buildup.text: Nutmeg grew only on the tiny Banda Islands in Indonesia — the world's sole source for centuries.

discovery.text: In medieval Europe, nutmeg was believed to cure plague. Prices reached astronomical levels.

twist.text: The Dutch traded Manhattan to Britain in exchange for Run Island — a nutmeg-producing speck of land.

climax.text: Eventually the British smuggled nutmeg trees to other colonies, breaking the Dutch monopoly forever.

punchline.text: New York was traded for a handful of nutmeg trees.

quiz.question: What did the Dutch trade to Britain in exchange for the nutmeg island of Run?

details.summary: The Dutch East India Company committed genocide on the Banda Islands in 1621 to monopolize nutmeg production, killing and enslaving nearly the entire population. Nutmeg was so valuable that the British traded Manhattan to the Dutch for the tiny nutmeg island of Run in 1667.
details.whyItMatters: Nutmeg's history reveals the extreme violence behind the spice trade. The same spice that flavors eggnog and béchamel drove some of colonialism's worst atrocities.
takeaways: The Dutch massacred Banda Islanders to control nutmeg supply
Britain traded Manhattan for the nutmeg island of Run in 1667
Myristicin in nutmeg is toxic in large doses but safe in cooking

faq.question: Why was nutmeg so valuable in the 17th century?
faq.answer: Nutmeg was believed to cure plague and was used to preserve food. It grew only on the tiny Banda Islands in Indonesia. This extreme geographic limitation combined with insatiable European demand made it worth more than gold by weight.

faq.question: Is nutmeg dangerous in large quantities?
faq.answer: Myristicin in nutmeg can cause hallucinations, nausea, and organ stress at doses above one to two tablespoons. Normal culinary use of a pinch or less is completely safe. Toxicity requires consuming quantities far beyond any recipe amount.
